claim: The scientist who gave us the word 'gas' also wrote a recipe for mice.

start.title: Fire
start.description: Rapid and hot oxidation of a material

end.title: Spontaneous generation
end.description: Theory of life arising from non-living matter

knots.passage: During the 17th century, a study of combustion was made by Jan Baptist van Helmont who discovered that burning charcoal released a gas sylvestris, or wild spirit. This was subsequently incorporated into Phlogiston theory by Johann Joachim Becher in 1667 and more formally by Georg Ernst Stahl in 1697; a concept that would strongly influence alchemical thinking for nearly two centuries.
knots.hatnote: Explaining fire took chemists centuries of wrong turns.

knots.passage: Van Helmont is regarded as the founder of pneumatic chemistry, as he was the first to understand that there are gases distinct in kind from atmospheric air and furthermore invented the word "gas". He derived the word gas from the Greek word chaos (χᾰ́ος).
knots.hatnote: Van Helmont gave science a word you use every day.

knots.passage: Van Helmont described a recipe for the spontaneous generation of mice (a piece of dirty cloth plus wheat for 21 days) and scorpions (basil, placed between two bricks and left in sunlight). His notes suggest he may have attempted to do these things.
knots.hatnote: Yet the same man wrote down something much stranger.

knots.passage: The ancient beliefs were subjected to testing. In 1668, the Italian physician and parasitologist Francesco Redi challenged the idea that maggots arose spontaneously from rotting meat. In the first major experiment to challenge spontaneous generation, he placed meat in a variety of sealed, open, and partially covered containers. Realizing that the sealed containers were deprived of air, he used "fine Naples veil", and observed no worms on the meat, but they appeared on the cloth.
knots.hatnote: Within a generation, someone tested such ideas properly.

knots.passage: Louis Pasteur's experiment's in the late 1850s are widely seen as having settled the question of spontaneous generation. He boiled a meat broth in a swan neck flask; the bend in the neck of the flask prevented falling particles from reaching the broth, while still allowing the free flow of air. The flask remained free of growth for an extended period. When the flask was turned so that particles could fall down the bends, the broth quickly became clouded.
knots.hatnote: The idea clung on for nearly two centuries, until a flask with a bent neck.

payoff: The man who named gas wrote a recipe for mice; Redi's veiled meat began the fightback and Pasteur's swan-neck flask finished it.
